paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All right, let's talk about the desire realm, which is where we are. It's divided into 20 parts. The Abhidharma is really boring — if you don't like lists of things — because it's the list of everything. Every category of everything is listed. We're mainly going to focus on these 20 categories in this course: all the different kinds of beings there are — all your friends, all your enemies, and all the ones you don't care about at all.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So there are 20 parts. There are eight hot hells. There's no pictures for these, I'm sorry — we're going to get to the pictures later. This is one of the cool things about AI: we don't really know what it looks like, so AI works great. There are eight hot hells. There's this thing called craving spirits — and by the way, we cannot see these beings; we can't perceive them directly. After craving spirits, there are animals, which we can perceive. There are humans of the four continents. And then there are six types of pleasure beings of the desire realm. Most of these beings we cannot see. "Well, where are they, Tim? Are they up, down, here — where are they?" We'll talk about it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What do we mean by the four continents? In Buddhism there are four different areas where humans live, and they have different types of life. The one we live on is the southern continent. Don't worry about it too much.

chapters.title: Where's the Nose? — How the Mind Assembles Your World

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What did I mean by this slide? Sorry — I made this one this afternoon, I was so jet-lagged. You know you're so tired when your eyes don't work together? Do you know that your eyes actually see two different things, and then your brain merges them together into one thing? You're actually looking at the world from two perspectives.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Seriously, try it — close one eye and look straight ahead. Focus on my nose. Now switch to the other eye. Did the nose move? Yes. So where is the nose? Is the nose in a fixed place? Your one eye sees the nose in one place, your other eye sees it in another place — but when you open both eyes, you just see one nose. So how many noses are there? You think there's just one nose there. But you just proved with your eyes that the nose is not in the same place.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: "Oh, but that's just a different perspective, Tim." Really? Is it just perspective? Why does your brain put the nose where your brain thinks the nose is? This way it's here, that way it's here — so the brain goes, "well then, it must be here." You're laughing, but you're realizing: the world is like that exploding-head emoji. You're already seeing something that's not there — and you think the nose is there. You're already a crazy person, and you thought you were sane. Sorry to break it to you. Where's the nose? Whose nose?

chapters.title: The Desire Realm — Everything Can Create a Mental Affliction

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So why do I have this picture up? The thing about the desire realm is that, unfortunately, every existing thing in it has the capacity to create a negative emotion in you. More specifically, every single thing that exists in the desire realm has this quality: it can create mental afflictions, from which non-virtue can develop.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: "Tim, what does that definition mean? Say it in clear English, please." Every single thing you can perceive in the desire realm — meaning everything in your world — has the ability for you to plant a bad seed with it. Even inanimate objects.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Like the other day, I was at the grocery store, opening up the refrigerator to buy eggs. And they told me: buy one, get one free — not one egg, but the whole carton. So I went back to get the second carton. I get there and I open up the door — and who has the door flat on the ground? Normally there's a space between the door and the floor. But some genius engineer decided it would look really nice to design the door all the way down to the floor. I walk up to get my free eggs — buy one, get one free — I'm feeling really good, 24 eggs for the price of 12. And eggs are really expensive in the United States, because they had this thing where they had to kill the chickens — it was ridiculous, and very sad — so the price is only now starting to come down as the number of chickens grows back. Organic chicken eggs. So I'm in a good mood — not only was the price low, but I get twice as many for the same price. This is how you sell to Tim.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I go to open the door, I walk up like this — remember what the engineer did — and I ran the door right over my toe, because I was wearing sandals, since it was 40 degrees outside. I'm sorry, Chinese medicine, but I don't wear socks when it's 40 degrees out. So the door scraped right over my toe. And then what did I do? I said some very nasty words. And it hurt. And I got pissed off. "Freaking free eggs." Stupid engineer, blah blah blah — I yelled at the door. "I'm going to complain to the manager. They hurt my toe."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: An inanimate object created a mental affliction. And that's every single thing in your universe, in the desire realm — it has the possibility of creating a negative affliction. Everything has the ability to create a bad seed. So that's what the desire realm is all about.

chapters.title: Food and Sex — the Two Drives of the Desire Realm

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And what do we mean by desire? Hold on, before you go to the next slide, Brian — let me make sure there are no kids here. Next slide. The desire realm. This is the best picture ever. What are the two characteristics of the desire realm? Food and sex. I love this picture.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: We're primarily motivated by these two things: the desire for food, and the desire for sex, at all different levels. And I'm not trying to say you're obsessed, or that you have addictions and things like that. But if you really watch the beings of the desire realm — most of them, most animals — what drives them to do things? They're looking for food. They're in a constant search for food.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Like — I not only adopted a third cat, but now apparently there's a fourth one outside that wants to live in the house. Apparently I'm just attracting zoos; animals just like me or something. But this cat is looking for food.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And cats are a really good example of the next part of the desire realm — sex. When a female cat goes into heat, and she's ovulating and ready to make babies, she releases a very potent pheromone, and all these hormones flood her body. And a female cat changes entirely — if you've ever witnessed it, it's like a completely different animal. And then that pheromone goes out into the world, and the male cats smell it, and they go completely, 100% insane. They try to get out of the house. The only thing they're focused on is sex — single-pointed shamatha. And they have no control over it. The females have no control over what's happening to their body; the males have no control. They're compelled to engage. Completely obsessed with that one thing.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I had a friend who was horseback riding. There's only a certain period when a male horse can have a female rider. So my friend gets on this horse, and they start riding, and within about 15 seconds the horse goes crazy and starts running — running as fast as he can. She can't stop it; she can barely turn it. Completely, 100% insane. And this horse is now running down the road toward the highway, and it jumps over a fence. She's thinking, "oh my God, we're going to die." So what she did was pull the horse to the left, to the side of the road, where there was a little ditch — she pulled him into the ditch, and he fell. He was so completely insane, running so fast, that he didn't even realize he was going to fall. And she timed it perfectly: as the horse tripped, she jumped off. She was a little hurt, but she was fine.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Then her friend, who was a much more experienced rider, came running up and realized the mistake, and asked her, "are you on your period right now?" She said yes. And the friend was like, "oh shit." That male horse had reached sexual maturity essentially that very day — and my friend happened to be menstruating. Even across a different species, the horse could smell the changes in her body, and was trying to find it, not realizing the person was sitting on top of him. So he ran. Completely gone. No control.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Then her friend said, "now get on my horse, and I'll get on this other horse." Second lesson: "you have to get back on a horse right now, because you fell off." She asked, "why?" Because if you don't get back on a horse right now, you'll never get on a horse again. What happens is, overnight, her brain would replay the accident, and it would generate a fear — a fear that would be almost impossible to overcome. So you have to have a positive experience right afterward. Which is also why it's so difficult to change behavior learned as a child: you have to have consistent, different kinds of experiences to train your nervous system not to have the same reaction. So she got back on the horse, and she was fine.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But that drive is so powerful. And somehow, as humans, we think we have more control over it. Obviously we don't go into those states the way cats and horses do — but we're not that far from it, right? What do you do most of the day? "When's my next meal? What are we going to have for breakfast tomorrow morning? What time do I have to go to breakfast, so I can have a meeting? What am I going to eat tomorrow? I hope they have my favorite food." I even asked them to buy me some food so I can make some simple lunches while I'm here. I'm eating a little differently these days — I don't know if you noticed, but I lost 8 kilos since the last time I was here — because I learned to eat better. I'll teach you someday if you'd like. I'm still learning, though; I still eat things I shouldn't, but less so.

chapters.title: Is Ice Cream Bad From Its Own Side? — Emptiness

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Even now, though, I'm eating things that are boring to eat. Healthy food. No sugar. I was good on the airplane — well, before I got on the airplane I was in the lounge, and they have these really delicious chocolate chip cookies. They're really big, but thin and chewy, and always warm, so the chocolate melts in your mouth. I didn't eat it. Why? Because I'd already decided I was going to eat something even better on the airplane. United Airlines has the best dessert cart ever. They have cheeses and things like that, which I don't like — but they have an ice cream bar. They serve this delicious vanilla ice cream, with chocolate sauce and caramel sauce and maraschino cherries. The only thing healthy about it was that I had the option to put peanuts on top.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But you see — I planned my own demise. Do you know how to say that? I planned my own failure. I knew I was going to eat something I shouldn't. Dairy is terrible for my body; I actually have an allergy to it. All that sugar — and I wonder why I couldn't sleep on the airplane. I planned eating terrible food. And I felt good about it, because I didn't eat the cookie. My virtue was that I didn't eat the cookie.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Let me tell you: if you're going to do something like that, at least enjoy it. There's a very special practice in the Diamond Way about enjoying things. So I'm going to ask you a very important question right now: is an ice cream sundae, with chocolate and caramel, bad for you from its own side?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: For most of us as humans, we have the seeds that a tremendous amount of sugar and dairy really is not good for us — I'm sorry, it's not. But is it bad from its own side? It has emptiness. Have you ever seen these really hot bodybuilder guys who eat really terrible food? And you're like, "that's not fair," right?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So I think there's a deep, deep Diamond Way practice of understanding that every single thing in the universe also has the possibility to create enlightenment — because of emptiness. Does that mean you should always eat ice cream sundaes? I didn't say that. But I want to plant that little seed in your mind: things aren't what they appear to be. The source of suffering can also be the source of enlightenment. If you understood anything I said tonight, let that seed germinate.
